draft.answer_text: For a red blood cell whose membrane is water permeable but impermeable to the relevant solutes, the extracellular solution's tonicity sets the direction of net water movement. In an isotonic solution, the extracellular fluid has the same osmolarity as the cell, and there is no net movement of water into or out of the cell [ev_004] [ev_001]; the cell keeps its normal volume and shape [ev_003]. In a hypertonic solution, the surrounding fluid has greater solute concentration than the cell, so water rushes out of the cell into the surrounding fluid and the red blood cell shrivels [ev_004] [ev_003]. In a hypotonic solution, the surrounding fluid has lower solute concentration than the cell, so water rushes into the red blood cell, causing it to swell and possibly rupture (lyse) [ev_004] [ev_003]. Water moves by osmosis, the diffusion of water through a semipermeable membrane, and the membrane limits the solutes' diffusion [ev_006] [ev_008]. Regarding your question: no, "no net water movement" in an isotonic solution does not mean individual water molecules stop crossing the membrane. The source states that there is no net movement of water into or out of the cell, although water will still move in and out [ev_004].

selected_source_quotes.exact_text: FIGURE 3.21 In osmosis, water always moves from an area of higher concentration (of water) to one of lower concentration (of water). In this system, the solute cannot pass through the selectively permeable membrane. A principle of diffusion is that the molecules move around and will spread evenly throughout the medium if they can. However, only the material capable of getting through the membrane will diffuse through it. In this example, the solute cannot diffuse through the membrane, but the water can. Water has a concentration gradient in this system. Therefore, water will diffuse down its concentration gradient, crossing the membrane to the side where it is less concentrated. This diffusion of water through the membrane—osmosis—will continue until the concentration gradient of water goes to zero. Osmosis proceeds constantly in living systems. support.exact_text: A galvanic cell based on the spontaneous reaction between copper and silver(I) is depicted in Figure 17.3.
The half-cell shown at the left contains the Cu(0)/Cu(II) couple in the form of a solid copper foil and an aqueous solution of copper nitrate.
By definition, the anode of an electrochemical cell is the electrode at which oxidation occurs (in this case, the Cu foil) and the cathode is the electrode where reduction occurs (the Ag foil).

four_frozen_facet_review.frozen_fact: Silver electrode is the cathode and silver ions are reduced.

support.exact_text: The right half-cell contains the Ag(I)/Ag(0) couple as solid silver foil and an aqueous silver nitrate solution.
By definition, the anode of an electrochemical cell is the electrode at which oxidation occurs (in this case, the Cu foil) and the cathode is the electrode where reduction occurs (the Ag foil).

four_frozen_facet_review.frozen_fact: External wire electron flow is from copper anode to silver cathode.

support.exact_text: Direct transfer of electrons is, therefore, prevented; transfer, instead, takes place indirectly through an external circuit that contacts the separated reactants.
A galvanic cell based on the spontaneous reaction between copper and silver(I) is depicted in Figure 17.3.
An external circuit is connected to each half-cell at its solid foil, meaning the Cu and Ag foil each function as an electrode.
By definition, the anode of an electrochemical cell is the electrode at which oxidation occurs (in this case, the Cu foil) and the cathode is the electrode where reduction occurs (the Ag foil).

These observations are consistent with (i) the oxidation of elemental copper to yield copper(II) ions, Cu2+(aq), which impart a blue color to the solution, and (ii) the reduction of silver(I) ions to yield elemental silver, which deposits as a fluffy solid on the copper wire surface.
And so, the direct transfer of electrons from the copper wire to the aqueous silver ions is spontaneous under the employed conditions.

four_frozen_facet_review.frozen_fact: The salt bridge transports inert ions to maintain charge balance; electron carriers in the wire differ from ion carriers in the bridge.

support.exact_text: To keep the reactants separate while maintaining charge-balance, the two half-cell solutions are connected by a tube filled with inert electrolyte solution called a salt bridge.

The spontaneous reaction in this cell produces Cu2+ cations in the anode half-cell and consumes Ag+ ions in the cathode half-cell, resulting in a compensatory flow of inert ions from the salt bridge that maintains charge balance.

Increasing concentrations of Cu2+ in the anode half-cell are balanced by an influx of NO3− from the salt bridge, while a flow of Na+ into the cathode half-cell compensates for the decreasing Ag+ concentration.
Direct transfer of electrons is, therefore, prevented; transfer, instead, takes place indirectly through an external circuit that contacts the separated reactants.

four_frozen_facet_review.frozen_fact: Adding H2 lowers Qc relative to Kc and causes temporary net forward/right reaction, consuming I2 and producing HI.

support.exact_text: When the system is at equilibrium, If reactant is added (increasing the denominator of the reaction quotient) or product is removed (decreasing the numerator), then Qc < Kc and the equilibrium will shift right.

If H2 is added, the right shift will consume I2 and produce HI as equilibrium is re-established, yielding a mixture with a greater concentrations of H2 and HI and a lesser concentration of I2 than was present before.

If the system is stressed by adding reactant, either H2 or I2, the resulting increase in concentration causes the rate of the forward reaction to increase, exceeding that of the reverse reaction: The system will experience a temporary net reaction in the forward direction to re-establish equilibrium (the equilibrium will shift right).

four_frozen_facet_review.frozen_fact: Removing HI also lowers Qc relative to Kc and causes temporary net forward/right reaction during restoration.

support.exact_text: When the system is at equilibrium, If reactant is added (increasing the denominator of the reaction quotient) or product is removed (decreasing the numerator), then Qc < Kc and the equilibrium will shift right.
This same shift will result if some product HI is removed from the system, which decreases the rate of the reverse reaction, again resulting in the same imbalance in rates.

four_frozen_facet_review.frozen_fact: At fixed temperature these concentration stresses do not change Kc.

support.exact_text: Despite these differences in composition, the value of the equilibrium constant will be the same after the stress as it was before (per the law of mass action).

four_frozen_facet_review.frozen_fact: Rightward restoration after HI removal does not imply final HI above its pre-removal value: in the textbook stated case final concentrations of all three species, including HI, are lower.

support.exact_text: Finally, if HI is removed, the concentrations of all three species will be lower when equilibrium is reestablished.

draft.answer_text: Adding H2 is a stress that increases the reactant concentration, so Qc falls below Kc and the equilibrium shifts right: the system has a temporary net forward reaction that consumes I2 and produces HI until equilibrium is re-established [ev_001] [ev_002]. The resulting mixture has greater concentrations of H2 and HI and a lesser concentration of I2 than before the addition [ev_001]. Removing HI is a separate stress that lowers the product concentration, so Qc falls below Kc and the temporary net reaction is also forward (right) [ev_001] [ev_002]. Because removing HI decreases the numerator of the reaction quotient, the equilibrium shifts right to replace some of the lost HI [ev_001] [ev_002]. The value of Kc does not change in either case: the equilibrium constant is the same after the stress as before, per the law of mass action [ev_001]. Compared with the HI concentration just before HI was removed, the final HI concentration after equilibrium is re-established is lower, since the source states that removing HI leaves the concentrations of all three species lower when equilibrium is reestablished [ev_001]. The source does not give a numerical comparison, so no quantitative ratio is stated.

four_frozen_facet_review.frozen_fact: Leading strand synthesis is continuous toward the fork; lagging synthesis makes Okazaki fragments away from the fork, each new fragment still synthesized 5-prime to 3-prime.

support.exact_text: Only one new DNA strand, the one that is complementary to the 3' to 5' parental DNA strand, can be synthesized continuously towards the replication fork.
This continuously synthesized strand is known as the leading strand.

The other strand, complementary to the 5' to 3' parental DNA, is extended away from the replication fork, in small fragments known as Okazaki fragments, each requiring a primer to start the synthesis.

The strand with the Okazaki fragments is known as the lagging strand.) The leading strand can be extended from a single primer, whereas the lagging strand needs a new primer for each of the short Okazaki fragments.
The strand with the Okazaki fragments is known as the lagging strand.

four_frozen_facet_review.frozen_fact: In bacteria DNA polymerase I removes RNA primers and fills the gaps with DNA.

support.exact_text: As synthesis proceeds, the RNA primers are replaced by DNA.

The primers are removed by the exonuclease activity of DNA pol I, which uses DNA behind the RNA as its own primer and fills in the gaps left by removal of the RNA nucleotides by the addition of DNA nucleotides.

four_frozen_facet_review.frozen_fact: DNA ligase seals remaining nicks by phosphodiester linking adjacent DNA segments.

support.exact_text: The nicks that remain between the newly synthesized DNA (that replaced the RNA primer) and the previously synthesized DNA are sealed by the enzyme DNA ligase, which catalyzes the formation of phosphodiester linkages between the 3'-OH end of one nucleotide and the 5' phosphate end of the other fragment.

The new strand complementary to the 3' to 5' parental strand can be synthesized continuously toward the replication fork; this is the leading strand [ev_001]. The other new strand, complementary to the 5' to 3' parental strand, is extended away from the replication fork in small fragments called Okazaki fragments, and each fragment needs its own primer to start synthesis; this is the lagging strand [ev_001] [ev_007]. The leading strand can be extended from a single primer, whereas the lagging strand needs a new primer for each short Okazaki fragment [ev_001]. The overall direction of the lagging strand is 3' to 5', and that of the leading strand is 5' to 3' [ev_002]. The remaining nicks between the newly synthesized DNA and the previously synthesized DNA are sealed by DNA ligase, which forms phosphodiester linkages between the 3'-OH end of one nucleotide and the 5' phosphate end of the adjacent fragment [ev_002].
